title: Binary search trees

INTRODUCTION

I. Prerequisites
Before starting with binary search trees (BST), the source states that you should have completed the binary tree playlist. Specifically, you must be familiar with the following four techniques:
  • In-order traversal
  • Pre-order traversal
  • Post-order traversal
  • Level order traversal
II. Definition of a Binary Search Tree (BST)
In a regular binary tree, it does not matter what node is on the left or the right. However, in a binary search tree, the position of the nodes matters significantly:

  • The Left Node: The "left guy" should be lesser than the node.
  • The Right Node: The "right guy" should be greater than the node.
  • No Equality: Generally, there is no "equal to" condition in a standard BST.
  • Recursive Condition: The entire left subtree must in itself be a BST, and the entire right subtree must in itself also be a BST.
III. Example Analysis
The source provides a specific example of a binary tree to illustrate why it qualifies as a BST:
  • Root Node (8): Everything on the left (3, 1, 6, 4, 7) is lesser than 8, and everything on the right (10, 14, 13) is greater than 8.
  • Subtree at Node 3: The left guy is 1 (smaller than 3) and the right guy is 6 (greater than 3).
  • Subtree at Node 6: The left guy is 4 (smaller than 6) and the right guy is 7 (greater than 6).
  • Subtree at Node 10: The right guy is 14 (greater than 10).
  • Subtree at Node 14: The left guy is 13 (smaller than 14).
IV. Handling Duplicates
While ideally duplicates are not allowed in a BST, the source notes that there are ways to integrate them if necessary:
  • Modified Condition: One could slightly change the logic to L≥N (left node greater than or equal to the node) and R>N.

  • Additional Nodes: You could add another left node to accommodate the duplicate value.
  • Counter/Frequency: Instead of adding nodes, a single node can store a counter (node, frequency) to track how many times a variable occurs.[8,2]
either integrate anotehr node o r maintain a node , frequency 
V. Why Use a Binary Search Tree?
The source compares BSTs to regular binary trees (BT) to highlight their efficiency:
  • Degenerate Trees: In a standard binary tree, you can have a "degenerate tree" (where nodes only have one child, like a linked list), resulting in a search time complexity of O(n).
  • Height Efficiency: In a BST, the height is generally kept as log2​n because the height difference between the left and right subtrees is kept as minimal as possible.
  • Search Speed: While searching in a binary tree requires a full traversal (O(n)), a BST allows you to find a node in logn time.
VI. Logic of the Search (The "Binary Search" in BST)
The name "Binary Search Tree" comes from the fact that searching the tree mimics a binary search:
  • Example (Searching for x = 6):
    1. Compare 6 to the root (8). Since 6 is smaller, you know it can never appear on the right side of the root. You move left.
    2. Compare 6 to the next node (3). Since 6 is greater, you know it will not be on the left. You move right.
  • By knowing the value must appear either on the left or the right, you eliminate half the search space at each step.

Search in a Binary Search Tree

I. Introduction to the Problem
The goal is to solve the problem of searching within a binary search tree (BST).
  • Input: You are given a node with a specific value (for example, the value 10).
  • Output: You need to return the reference or the address (the entire node) that contains this value.
  • Edge Case: If the value does not exist in the tree, you must return null.
II. Binary Tree vs. Binary Search Tree Efficiency
The source highlights the difference in search performance between these two structures:
  • Binary Tree: If this were a regular binary tree, you would have to perform a traversal (in-order, pre-order, post-order, or level order) and check every node. This search would end up taking O(n) time.
  • Binary Search Tree: In almost every BST provided, the search time is logarithmic, specifically log2​n height, because of the tree's properties.
III. The BST Search Property
The search logic relies on the fundamental property that the left is always lesser than the current node and the right is always greater than the current node.
IV. Step-by-Step Example: Searching for Value 10
The source provides a specific walkthrough of the search process starting at a root node of 8:
  1. Start at 8: Since 8 is not equal to 10, your brain knows the left part is lesser than 8 and the right part is greater than 8.
  2. Decide Direction: Since 10 is greater than 8, it must lie on the "greater part" (the right).
  3. Move to 12: You move to the right and end up at 12. This is not equivalent to 10.
  4. Decide Direction: Again, look at the left (smaller) and right (greater). Since 10 is smaller than 12, it should lie on the left part.
  5. Move to 10: You move left and end up at 10. Since this is equivalent to the desired value, you take the entire node and return it.
V. Example: Searching for a Non-Existent Value (Value 9)
  • If you were searching for 9, the moment you reached 10, you would see they are not equivalent.
  • Since 9 is smaller than 10, you would move left.
  • In this example, moving left from 10 leads to null.
  • Whenever you reach null, you return null.
VI. Complexity Analysis
  • Traversing the Height: You are not traversing the entire tree; you are traversing "somewhere around the height of the tree".
  • Time Complexity: Because you only move either left or right at each step, you end up going to a leaf node in the worst case. Therefore, the time complexity is the height of the tree, which is O(log2​n).   
  • in bst height is alaways olog2n
  • Advantage: This is the primary advantage of a BST over a binary tree—you avoid traversing all nodes.
VII. Implementation Logic (C++ and Java)
The source describes the programmatic approach:
  • Traversal Condition: Keep traversing as long as you haven't reached null AND the current root value does not coincide with the value you are looking for.
  • Directional Logic:
    • If the target value is lesser than the current root value, move left.
    • Otherwise, move right.
  • Termination: If a match is found, the loop stops and the node is returned. If the value is not there, the loop ends when the root becomes null, and it returns null.

Inserting a Node into a Binary Search Tree 

I. Problem Statement and Basic Requirements
The objective is to insert a given value (for example, the value 5) into a binary search tree (BST). The insertion must be performed such that the fundamental properties of a BST are maintained:
  • The left is smaller than the node.
  • The right is greater than the node.
  • The left subtree is a BST, and the right subtree is a BST.
  • Once the insertion is complete, you return the root of the modified binary tree.
II. Multiple Possibilities for Insertion
The source notes that there can be multiple ways to insert a node while still maintaining BST properties.
  • Insertion at a Leaf: You can find an available leaf position and insert the node there.
  • Insertion Between Nodes: For example, if you have values 4 and 7, you could potentially insert 5 in between them.
  • The problem asks you to find and return any one valid modification of the tree.

multiple poisibilites 
III. The Simplified Logic: Finding the Leaf Position
To avoid complicating the problem, the recommended approach is to "insert the node at whichever leaf it is possible". This involves trying to figure out where that value "ideally would have been" if it were already in the tree.
  • Example (Value 5): Start at the root. If 5 is on the right, move right. If the next node is 7 and 5 should be on the left, but nothing exists there, insert it into that left null position.
  • Example (Value 0): Start at the root. 0 should be on the left. If the next node is 2, move left. If the next node is 1, move left. Since nothing exists there, insert 0 into the left of 1.
  • Example (Value 9): Start at the root. 9 should be on the right. Move to the next node (7). 9 should be on the right. Since there is nothing on the right of 7, insert it there.
  • Crucial Rule: The value being inserted will always be a new value that does not already exist in the BST. The insertion point will "always be some leaf position".
IV. Programmatic Implementation Logic
The logic for the code is described as follows:
  1. Check for Empty Tree: If the root is null, the new node itself becomes the root, and you return it.
  2. Create a Copy: Create a copy of the root (referred to as cur or curr) so that you can return the original root at the end of the process.
  3. Traverse the Tree: Keep traversing the tree to find the correct spot.
    • Right Side: If the target value is greater than the current node's value:
      • If the right child is not null, move the curr pointer to the right.
      • If the right child is null, create a new node with the value, point the right side to it, and break the loop.
    • Left Side: If the target value is smaller than the current node's value:
      • If the left child is not null, move the curr pointer to the left.
      • If the left child is null, create a new node, insert it there, and break.
  4. Return: Finally, return the original root of the modified tree.
V. Dry Run Example
The source provides a dry run searching for value 5 in a tree where the root is 6:
  1. At Root (6): 5 is not greater than 6, so you move to the left child (3).
  2. At Node (3): 5 is greater than 3, so you check the right child.
  3. At Node (4): The current pointer moves to 4. 5 is greater than 4, but 4's right child is null.
  4. Insertion: You point 4's right child to a new node containing the value 5 and then break the loop.
VI. Time Complexity
Assuming the binary search tree is height-balanced, the time complexity for this insertion operation is O(log2​n).

I. Definition of a Binary Search Tree (BST)

Before beginning the deletion process, the source reiterates the property of a BST:
  • The left should be lesser than the node.
  • The right should be greater than the node.
  • The entire subtree must itself be a BST.
II. The Problem Goal
  • Task: You are given a node to delete.
  • Requirement: After deleting the node, you must perform a rearrangement to form a valid BST and maintain all BST properties.
III. The Core Deletion Logic (Restructuring)
The source suggests a strategy of dividing the tree into parts after a node is removed:
  • The Left and Right Portions: When a node is deleted, you are left with a left subtree and a right subtree that were originally attached to that node.
  • The Connection Strategy: To keep the tree as a BST, you take the entire right subtree and attach it to the extreme right of the left subtree.
  • Reasoning: The "extreme right" of the left subtree is the greatest element in that left portion. Since every element in the right subtree is greater than every element in the left subtree, the right subtree can safely be attached to the right of the left subtree's largest element.

The source uses a visual example to explain the connection:

  2. Assume you have a right subtree starting with 5.
  3. To merge them, you make sure the extreme right (4) of the left subtree is connected to the right subtree (5).
  4. Specifically, you "take this right portion and connect it to 4".
V. Programmatic Implementation Logic
The deletion is handled in two main parts: finding the node and then using a helper function to delete it.
Part A: Finding the Node
  1. Check Null: If the root is null, return null.
  2. Check Root: If the root's value is the key to be deleted, call the helper function on the root and return the result.
  3. Traverse:
    • If the key is greater than the current root value, move to the right. If the right child's value matches the key, set the right child to the result of the helper function.
    • If the key is lesser than the current root value, move to the left. If the left child's value matches the key, set the left child to the result of the helper function.
Part B: The Helper Function (helper)
This function performs the actual deletion and restructuring:
  1. Case 1 (Left is Null): If the node's left child is null, simply return the right child.
  2. Case 2 (Right is Null): If the node's right child is null, simply return the left child.
  3. Case 3 (Both Exist):
    • Save the right child.
    • Find the "last right" (the extreme right node) of the left subtree.
    • Point the right of this "last right" node to the saved right child.
    • Return the left subtree.
VI. Complexity Analysis
  • Time Complexity: The complexity is O(H) (where H is the height of the tree) because you are searching for the node and then performing a constant time connection.
  • Space Complexity: The source states there is no external space used (beyond the recursion stack), making it efficient.

I. Problem Overview: K-th Smallest Element

The goal is to solve the problem of finding the k-th smallest element in a given binary search tree (BST).
  • Example Tree: You are given a BST where 5 is the root, to the left is 3, then to the left of that is 1, then there is 2, and so on.
  • The Scenario: If all the elements of this BST were written in a proper sorted order, they would be: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
  • The Task: If the input k is 3, you need to figure out the third smallest element, which in this case is 3. You must return this value given the root of the tree.
II. The Naive Approach
The source describes a simple but inefficient way to solve the problem:
  1. Traversal: Perform any DFS traversal (in-order, post-order, or pre-order) to visit all nodes.
  2. Storage: Store all these nodes into a container, such as a vector (in C++) or a list (in Java).
  3. Sorting: Sort that container.
  4. Selection: Take the third smallest element (the third element from the front).
Problems with the Naive Approach:
  • Time Complexity: O(n) for traversal plus O(nlogn) if you decide to sort the entire container.
  • Space Complexity: O(n) extra space to store the entire BST into a container.
  • The Goal: The source states we want to eliminate the extra logn and avoid using O(n) extra space if possible.
III. The Efficient Approach (In-order Property)
A fundamental property of a Binary Search Tree is that its in-order traversal (Left, Root, Right) is always in sorted order.
  • Everything to the left of a node is smaller, and everything to the right is greater.
  • Example In-order: For the given tree, the in-order traversal results in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
  • By using in-order traversal, the extra O(nlogn) required for sorting is eliminated.
cause yeh left node right hota h or left chota usse bda node usse bda right toh yeh inorder me bhi yeh hi sequenc eaata h 
IV. Refining the Logic (Eliminating Extra Space)
To avoid the O(n) space required to store the nodes in a list or vector, the source suggests using a counter:
  1. Initialize: Keep a counter starting at 0.
  2. Logic: In-order traversal visits nodes in the sequence: Left -> Node/Root -> Right.
  3. Increment: Every time you "visit" a particular node (the "Root" step of the traversal), perform counter++.
  4. Check: At the moment the counter becomes equal to k, the node you are currently standing at is the k-th smallest element.

V. Traversal Techniques and Complexity
The source mentions three types of traversals where this counter logic can be inserted:
  • Recursive Traversal: Time complexity O(n); Space complexity O(n) (stack space).
  • Iterative Stack Traversal: Time complexity O(n); Space complexity O(n).
  • Morris Traversal: Time complexity O(n); Space complexity O(1).
VI. K-th Largest Element in a BST
The source explains how to adapt the logic if the question changes to finding the k-th largest element.
  • Logic: One simple traversal is performed to count the total number of nodes (n) in the tree.
  • The Formula: Finding the k-th largest is equivalent to saying you are finding the (n−k)-th smallest element.
  • Requirement: This requires two traversals: one to compute the total number of nodes and another to find the (n−k)-th smallest element using the in-order counter method.
I. Problem Definition

Validate a Binary Search Tree. 

  • BST Definition: By definition, everything to the left of a node must be smaller than that node, and everything to the right must be greater.
  • Recursive Property: This property must hold for every single node in the entire tree.

II. Why Local Checks are Insufficient
The source explains why you cannot simply check if a node is greater than its left child and smaller than its right child.
  • The Example: Consider a tree where the root is 5, its right child is 6, and the left child of 6 is 4.
  • The Conflict: Locally, 4 is on the left of 6, which is "okay" because 4 is smaller than 6. However, because 4 is in the right subtree of 5, it must be greater than 5.
  • The Result: Since 4 is not greater than 5, this is not a valid BST, even though the local condition at node 6 was satisfied.
III. The Intuition: Using Range Bounds
To solve this, you must provide a range to each particular node.
  • Concept: Every node should lie within a specific (min, max) interval. If a node's value falls outside this range, the tree is not a BST.
  • Initial Range: For the root, the initial range is from minus infinity to plus infinity (LONG_MIN to LONG_MAX), as all elements should ideally fall within this.
IV. Step-by-Step Example (Root 13)
The source walks through a valid BST with root 13 to show how ranges update:
  1. At Root (13): The range is (-inf, +inf). 13 is valid.
  2. Moving Left: Everything to the left must be smaller than 13. The new range becomes (-inf, 13).
    • Node 10: 10 is between -inf and 13, so it is valid.
    • Right of 10: Elements must be greater than 10 but still smaller than 13. The range is (10, 13). A node like 12 fits here and is valid.
  3. Moving Right: Everything to the right must be greater than 13. The new range becomes (13, +inf).
    • Node 15: 15 is valid in this range.
    • Left of 15: Elements must be greater than 13 but smaller than 15. The range is (13, 15). A node like 14 is valid here.
    • Right of 15: Elements must be greater than 15. The range is (15, +inf). A node like 17 is valid here.

V. Programmatic Implementation Logic
The code follows a simple recursive structure:
  • Function Signature: isValidBST(root, minVal, maxVal).
  • Base Case: If the current node is null, return true (a null tree is a valid BST).
  • Validation Check: If the root->val is less than or equal to minVal OR greater than or equal to maxVal, return false.
  • Recursive Calls:
    • For the left child, update the max boundary: isValidBST(root->left, minVal, root->val).
    • For the right child, update the min boundary: isValidBST(root->right, root->val, maxVal).
  • Final Return: The function returns true only if both the left and right calls return true.
VI. Complexity Analysis
  • Time Complexity: O(N) because we perform a traversal and visit every node exactly once.
  • Space Complexity: O(N) because of the auxiliary stack space used during the recursive calls.

Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) in a Binary Search Tree 


II. Definition of Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)

LCA is defined based on the paths from the nodes to the root:

  • Example 1 (LCA of 5 and 0): If you draw down the path for 5 till the root and the path for 0 till the root, the first intersection point (if looking from the bottom) or the last intersection point (if looking from the top) is what the LCA will be.
  • Example 2 (LCA of 2 and 5): The LCA is the first intersection point in the paths of 2 and 5.

III. Naive Approach vs. BST Approach

  • Naive Approach: Finding LCA in a regular binary tree takes a time complexity of $O(n)$, representing the traversal time. 0(N) big of n lgta tha isme ;

IV. The Logic of Possibilities

When standing at a node while looking for two nodes (U and V), there are a few possibilities:

  1. Both lie to the right.
  2. Both lie to the left.
  3. One lies to the left and one lies to the right.
  4. The node itself is one among them.

V. The "Split Point" Intuition

The source explains that the LCA is the point where the paths to the two target nodes finally diverge:

  • The Logic: The last point where you can say one node lies on the left and the other lies on the right is your LCA.
  • Example (LCA of 5 and 9 in a tree where root is 10):
    1. At 10: Both 5 and 9 are smaller than 10, so you move to the left because you "surely know that this is the path that you have to move next".
    2. At 4: Both 5 and 9 are greater than 4, so you move to the right.
    3. At 8: 5 is on the left and 9 is on the right. This is the moment the "path split.".
    4. Result: The last point of the split is what your LCA will be (Node 8).

VI. Example: LCA of 1 and 2

  • At 10: Both lie on the left.
  • At 4: Both lie on the left.
  • Termination: The moment you cannot say both are on the left or both are on the right (or one is the node itself), that guy is the LCA.
  • General Rule: If both are on the left, you move left; if both are on the right, you move right. The moment that is not the case, you have found the LCA.

VII. Complexity Analysis

  • Time Complexity: You move left or right, traversing the height of the tree. Therefore, the complexity is $O(H)$ (height of the tree).
  • Generic BST: In a generic BST, $O(H)$ is "much, much better" than $O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: The complexity is $O(1)$ if you use a normal while loop (avoiding the recursion stack space).

VIII. Implementation Logic

The programmatic logic for the recursive approach (identical for C++ and Java) is as follows:

  1. Check Null: If the root is null, do nothing/return null.
  2. Move Right: If both target nodes (P and Q) have values greater than the root, go to the right subtree.
  3. Move Left: If both target nodes have values smaller than the root, go to the left subtree.
  4. Return: If you cannot determine that both are on the left or both are on the right, return the current root as the first point of intersection.

 Constructing a Binary Search Tree from Pre-order Traversal 


I. Problem Introduction and Definition
The task is to solve the problem of constructing a binary search tree (BST) from a given pre-order traversal.
  • Definition of BST: If you have a node, everything to the left of that node will be smaller than this node's value, and everything to the right will be greater.
  • The Input: You are given a pre-order traversal sequence, for example: 8, 5, 1, 7, 10, 12.
  • The Output: You must draw the corresponding BST and return the root of that tree.
II. The Brute Force Method
The "brute way" is to manually and naively create the tree node by node.
  • Pre-order Property: Pre-order follows the sequence: Root (or Node), Left, Right.
  • Example Walkthrough (8, 5, 1, 7, 10, 12):
    1. Initial Node: 8 is the root.
    2. Next Value (5): Since 5 is smaller than 8, it is inserted on the left of 8.
    3. Next Value (1): 1 is smaller than 8 (left) and smaller than 5 (left), so 1 is inserted on the left of 5.
    4. Next Value (7): 7 is smaller than 8 (left) but greater than 5, so it is inserted on the right of 5.
    5. Next Value (10): 10 is greater than 8, so it goes to the right.
    6. Next Value (12): 12 is greater than 8, so it goes to the right of 10 (like "tapping" onto the tree).
  • Brute Force Complexity:
    • Time Complexity: For every node, you determine left or right. In the worst case (like a skewed tree), this takes O(n2) (n×n).
    • Space Complexity: No external space is used apart from the space needed to create the tree itself.
III. The "Better" Method (Using In-order Property)
A binary search tree's in-order traversal is always sorted.
  1. Sorting: Take the given pre-order nodes and sort them to get the in-order traversal (e.g., 1, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12).
  2. Unique Construction: Using the pre-order and the sorted in-order, you can create a unique binary tree, which will be the BST.
  3. Better Method Complexity:
    • Time Complexity: Sorting takes O(nlogn), and creating the BST from the two traversals takes another O(n).
    • Space Complexity: O(n) to store the in-order traversal in a container like a vector or list.
IV. The Efficient Method (Upper Bound Logic)
The efficient method achieves the construction in O(n) time by using range bounds.

  • Refinement: You do not actually need to carry the lower bound; you only need the upper bound.

    • Moving Left: When you go left, the upper bound becomes the node's value because you cannot exceed it.
    • Moving Right: When you go right, you pass on the same upper bound that the current node had.
    • Lower Bound Check: If a value (e.g., 7) cannot be planted at a certain spot (because it's greater than the current upper bound), it automatically handles the lower bound logic.
V. Efficient Example Walkthrough (8, 5, 1, 7, 10, 12)
  1. At 8: Upper bound is INT_MAX. 8 is within bounds. 8 becomes root.
  2. Go Left: Upper bound is now 8. Pointer moves to 5. 5 < 8, so 5 is valid.
  3. Go Left from 5: Upper bound is 5. Pointer moves to 1. 1 < 5, so 1 is valid.
  4. Go Left from 1: Upper bound is 1. Pointer moves to 7. 7 > 1, so this returns null.
  5. Go Right from 1: Upper bound remains 5. 7 > 5, so this returns null.
  6. Go Right from 5: Upper bound is 8. Pointer moves to 7. 7 < 8, so 7 is valid and placed on the right of 5.
  7. Go Right from 8: Upper bound remains INT_MAX. Pointer moves to 10. 10 < INT_MAX, so 10 is placed on the right of 8.
  8. Go Right from 10: Upper bound remains INT_MAX. Pointer moves to 12. 12 is placed on the right.

VI. Complexity and Implementation Details
  • Efficient Time Complexity: Each node is visited approximately three times (once from above, once returning from left, once returning from right). This is O(3n), which simplifies to O(n).
  • Efficient Space Complexity: Uses O(n) recursion stack space, but no external containers.
  • Implementation Logic:
    • Maintain a global pointer (index i) to track the current element in the pre-order array.
    • Build Function: Takes the vector/array, the pointer i, and the upper bound.
    • Base Cases: Return null if you run out of elements or if the current element is out of the upper bound.
    • Reference Handling: In C++, pass i by reference. In Java, since variables cannot be passed by reference, use an array of size one (index 0 as the variable) to move the pointer across the process.
